904.title: Akrura sees him in the river
904.hook: Akrura dives into the Yamuna and finds Krishna there too
904.carry: the lord is in the chariot and the river
904.howItsDone: Akrura's hymn in the Bhagavata is recited by devotees, and pilgrims bathe at a place on the Yamuna that tradition links with his vision.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: leaving Vrindavan, from the side of the ones who stay. The gopis in the road, a promise to come back, and the dust settling.
screen: `LEAVING VRINDAVAN.` · `UNTIL THE DUST IS GONE.`

segments.voice: On the road to Mathura, the chariot stops at the river. Akrura asks the boys to wait in the shade while he goes down to the Yamuna to bathe and say his prayers. He wades in, ducks under, and opens his eyes. Krishna and Balarama are there, under the river, looking at him. Which is strange, because he just left them sitting in the chariot.
screen: `THE CHARIOT STOPS AT THE RIVER.` → `AKRURA DUCKS UNDER.` → `THE BOYS ARE IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: He comes up for air and looks back at the bank. There's the chariot, and the two boys sitting in it, just as he left them. So he goes under again, and this time the vision is bigger. He sees Balarama as the great serpent Ananta, and resting on him, Vishnu himself, dark as a rain cloud, with sages singing his praise. Akrura stays there in the river, and the Bhagavata gives him a long hymn of praise. Then he climbs out, dripping, and walks back to the chariot in a daze. Krishna asks him, kindly, whether he's seen something wonderful, Akrura answers that every wonder there is, is in Krishna, and he's looking at him. Why put this scene here? The village has just watched Krishna leave. And on that same road, a man finds that the boy in the chariot is also in the river, and also beyond all of it. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, told as a story: the Lord isn't in one place. Vishnu's very name is often explained as the one who pervades everything. Hindus keep a murti at home and go to the temple to meet him there, but they don't believe that's the only place he is. The leaving is real; nobody in the story pretends it isn't. But many readers hear the river as the answer to the grief: the one who left the village hasn't left anything. They reach Mathura as the day ends, and Krishna walks into the city on foot, with the cowherds.
screen: `ON THE CHARIOT, AND IN THE RIVER.` · `VISHNU RESTING ON ANANTA.` · `EVERY WONDER IS IN YOU.` · `VISHNU: THE ONE WHO PERVADES EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `HE HASN'T LEFT ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: Akrura met the Lord while bathing and praying, and many Hindus still begin the day with water and a name. As you wash today, go slowly. If you pray, say softly, Om Namo Narayanaya, or Krishna's name, or the name of God you use, remembering he's in that water too. If you don't pray, just look at the water as if you'd come up from the river.

905.title: One boy, many eyes
905.hook: Krishna walks into Kamsa's arena, and everyone sees someone different
905.carry: krishna meets each heart the way it comes
905.howItsDone: The story of Krishna in Mathura and Kamsa's end is recited from the Bhagavata and staged in Krishna plays and festivals in the region of Mathura and Vrindavan.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Akrura went under the river and found Krishna there, and in the chariot at once. The Lord isn't in one place.
screen: `AKRURA SEES HIM IN THE RIVER.` · `THE LORD IS IN THE CHARIOT AND THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: King Kamsa can't sleep. That afternoon, word reached the palace that a cowherd boy walked into the festival hall, snapped the great bow on display, and fought off the guards. That night, the Bhagavata lists his omens. He looks at his reflection and can't see his head. He can't hear his own breath. He looks back for his footprints and finds none. The man who has spent the whole story hunting a child is now hunted, by his own mind.
screen: `THE GREAT BOW SNAPPED.` → `KAMSA CAN'T SLEEP.` → `NO HEAD IN THE REFLECTION.`

segments.voice: Morning brings the festival. Kamsa takes his seat high above the wrestling ground. His champion wrestlers are ready. And at the gate he's stationed a huge war elephant with orders to crush the boys. It doesn't work. Krishna fights the elephant, brings it down, and walks into the arena with one of its tusks on his shoulder, Balarama beside him. Then the Bhagavata stops the action and looks around the stands, one face at a time. To the wrestlers, Krishna looks like a thunderbolt. To the women, love itself in a body. To the cowherds, their kinsman. To unjust rulers, their punisher. To his parents, their child. To the yogis, the highest truth. To his own clan, their deity. And to Kamsa, the text says, he looks like death. Same boy, same moment. What each one sees depends on what each one brought in. Kamsa brought a lifetime of fear, and fear is what walks in. Krishna says it himself in the Bhagavad Gita: in whatever way people come to me, in that way I receive them. That's why Hindus love Krishna in so many ways at once. Some cradle him as a baby, the butter thief. Some love him as a friend, some as a beloved, some as the teacher on Arjuna's chariot. The tradition doesn't make you pick the correct one. The same Lord meets each heart the way it comes.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT AT THE GATE.` · `A TUSK ON HIS SHOULDER.` · `ONE BOY, MANY EYES.` · `TO KAMSA, HE LOOKS LIKE DEATH.` · then, large: `AS PEOPLE COME TO ME, SO I RECEIVE THEM.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus come to Krishna in one relationship that feels like theirs: a child to cuddle, a friend to tease, a beloved to long for, a teacher to listen to. Picture the form you feel closest to, or the God you know, and greet him that way. If you don't pray, notice what you're carrying toward one person today, and set it down at the gate for a few breaths.

906.title: The king who lived afraid
906.hook: Kamsa falls in his own arena, and reaches Krishna through fear
906.carry: a mind fixed on krishna reaches him
906.howItsDone: Kamsa's death and the freeing of Devaki and Vasudeva are retold from the Bhagavata, and Kamsa's defeat is acted out in festival performances in the Mathura area.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kamsa's arena began. A sleepless king, an elephant at the gate, and one boy seen many ways. Krishna meets each heart the way it comes.
screen: `ONE BOY, MANY EYES.` · `KRISHNA MEETS EACH HEART THE WAY IT COMES.`

segments.voice: The women in the stands aren't happy. Down on the wrestling ground, Kamsa's champion Chanura has squared off against Krishna, and his partner Mushtika against Balarama: giants against two boys from the pastures. The Bhagavata lets us hear the crowd. This is wrong, the women tell each other. It's no fair match. Whoever allowed it shares the blame. And the cowherd girls of Vraja were lucky, they say, to see him every day.
screen: `CHANURA AND MUSHTIKA.` → `TWO BOYS AGAINST GIANTS.` → `THE CROWD SAYS, THIS IS WRONG.`

segments.voice: The fight goes hold for hold, then turns. Krishna brings down Chanura, Balarama brings down Mushtika, and the other wrestlers fall or run. Kamsa orders the music stopped. He shouts for the boys to be driven out, and for Vasudeva and his own father Ugrasena to be killed. Before he finishes, Krishna is on the platform. Kamsa reaches for his sword. Krishna catches him by the hair, pulls him down into the arena, and it's over. Then the Bhagavata says something striking. All his life, eating, drinking, walking, sleeping, Kamsa thought of Krishna, out of fear. And because his mind was so fixed on him, the text says, he reached him in the end. It's the frame from the rasa lila: what matters is where the mind is turned, even by terror. Hindus take that seriously in daily life. It's why they keep God's name close: chanting it on beads, singing it, saying it when they're scared, and saying Rama's or Krishna's name beside someone who is dying. In the Gita, Krishna says whatever a person remembers at the end, that is where they go. Kamsa remembered Krishna by accident, out of dread. Devotees try to do it on purpose, out of love. Kamsa's wives come weeping, and Krishna comforts them and sees the funeral rites done. Then he frees his parents, Vasudeva and Devaki, and bows at their feet. So the story of his childhood closes where it began: a birth in a prison cell, and now the cell door open, and a son kneeling before his mother.
screen: `THE WRESTLERS FALL.` · `HE WAS NEVER NOT THINKING OF HIM.` · `KEEP THE NAME CLOSE.` · `KAMSA'S WIVES ARE COMFORTED.` · then, large: `THE PRISON DOOR OPENS.`

segments.voice: Hindus call this nama japa, repeating the name. Bring to mind one small fear you've been carrying. Then, with each slow breath, say one name of God softly: Krishna, or Rama, or the name you use. Let the fear and the name sit together, the way they did in Kamsa, but turned toward love. If you don't pray, choose one steady word and let it carry each breath.
Kamsa's death. The king who spent his life afraid of Krishna, pulled down in his own arena, and reaching him, the text says, through his fear.

907.title: Andal's garland
907.hook: a girl tries on the garland meant for the god
907.carry: bhakti: love is the real offering
907.howItsDone: Andal is honored as one of the Alvars in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes; at Srivilliputtur, tradition holds that a garland worn by her image is still offered to the Lord.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the king who lived afraid. Fear kept Kamsa's mind on Krishna all his life, and a mind fixed on Krishna reaches him.
screen: `THE KING WHO LIVED AFRAID.` · `A MIND FIXED ON KRISHNA REACHES HIM.`

segments.voice: A garland of fresh flowers lies ready in a temple gardener's house, woven that morning for the image of Vishnu. While her father is out, his daughter picks it up and puts it around her own neck. Then she looks at her reflection and asks: would he want me? The he, for her, is the god the garland was made for. Today we meet the people who sang Krishna's story, in the Tamil south.
screen: `A GARLAND FOR THE GOD.` → `SHE TRIES IT ON FIRST.` → `WOULD HE WANT ME?`

segments.voice: The Alvars are the poet-saints of Vishnu who sang in Tamil. Tradition counts twelve, and explains the name as people sunk deep in God. Their songs are love songs, complaints, lullabies, longing. The girl with the garland is one of them: Andal. Her father, himself remembered as one of the Alvars, tends a flower garden for the temple. Tradition says he found her there as a baby, under a tulasi plant, and raised her as his own. She grows up on Krishna's stories and will marry no one but the Lord. So she wears the garland before it goes to the temple. One day her father catches her. He's horrified: a garland someone has worn can't be offered to God. He throws it out and weaves a new one. That night, the story says, the Lord comes to him in a dream and asks why the usual garland didn't arrive. The one she wore is the one he wants. From then on her garlands go to the temple after she's worn them, and she's called the girl who gave the garland she had worn. In Hindu worship the offering goes to God first. Flowers, food, a garland: you don't taste it, sniff it or try it on. Afterward it comes back to you as prasad, blessed, and you take it with both hands. Andal's story runs that order backward, and the tradition loves her for it. It didn't change the rule; families still offer fresh. But it shows what the rule is for. This is bhakti, the heart of the Alvars: what the Lord wants is love, and love is the real offering. Nammalvar, the other great Alvar, comes the day after tomorrow.
screen: `THE ALVARS: POETS SUNK DEEP IN GOD.` · `A BABY UNDER THE TULASI PLANT.` · `HER FATHER THROWS THE GARLAND OUT.` · `THE ONE SHE WORE IS THE ONE HE WANTS.` · then, large: `BHAKTI: LOVE IS THE OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal or drink, do what many Hindu families do. Set it down and offer it first, silently, to Krishna, or to God by whatever name you use. Then eat it as prasad, a gift given back to you. If you don't pray, pause for one breath of thanks before the first bite.

908.title: Girls knocking before dawn
908.hook: girls knocking on doors in the dark, waking each other up
908.carry: satsang: we go to krishna together
908.howItsDone: During the Tamil month of Margazhi, Andal's Tiruppavai is sung before dawn in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes, and the day's verse is often recited in morning worship.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars, and Andal, the gardener's daughter who wore the garland first. Bhakti: love is the real offering.
screen: `ANDAL'S GARLAND.` · `BHAKTI: LOVE IS THE REAL OFFERING.`

segments.voice: It's still dark, cold enough that nobody wants to leave the blanket. A group of girls goes from house to house, rapping on doors and calling through windows to friends still asleep. Get up. The birds are already talking. You said you'd come. Are you deaf, or just pretending? This isn't a diary. It's a poem: Andal's song cycle, the Tiruppavai.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, IN THE COLD.` → `KNOCKING ON FRIENDS' DOORS.` → `ANDAL'S TIRUPPAVAI.`

segments.voice: The Tiruppavai is set in the Tamil month of Margazhi, in the cold season. Andal imagines herself as one of the cowherd girls of Krishna's village, the same village we just left in the Bhagavata. The girls have taken a vow for the month: rise before dawn, bathe, keep simple, and go together to seek him. So the songs move like a morning. First they gather. Then they wake the girls who overslept, door by door, affectionate and funny, the way friends really talk. They arrive at the house of Nanda, Krishna's foster father. They wake the doorkeeper, then the family inside. At last they stand before Krishna and tell him why they've come. On the surface, for a drum, a ritual drum for their vow. Then the songs turn. The drum was an excuse. What they want is to belong to him, to serve him, not just today but in every life to come. Notice who's seeking here. Not a lone hermit in a cave: a gang of friends dragging each other out of bed, refusing to go without the one still asleep. Hindus have a word for this: satsang, the company of people turned toward God. In Andal's picture, nobody gets to the door alone, and nobody's left behind for being lazy. They just knock louder. That's why these songs aren't only read. In Margazhi, people in Tamil homes and temples sing them before sunrise, together. A poem about waking each other up became a reason to get up.
screen: `THE COLD MONTH OF MARGAZHI.` · `WAKING THE GIRLS WHO OVERSLEPT.` · `AT NANDA'S DOOR.` · `NOT A DRUM, BUT TO BELONG TO HIM.` · then, large: `SATSANG: NOBODY GOES ALONE.`

909.title: Nammalvar's riddle
909.hook: a silent boy under a tamarind tree, and a riddle that wakes him
909.carry: the self lives in the body, but isn't it
909.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas recite Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temple worship and at home, and the tamarind tree at his temple town is honored as the place where he sat.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars, and Andal's Tiruppavai, girls knocking on doors before dawn. Satsang: we go to Krishna together.
screen: `GIRLS KNOCKING BEFORE DAWN.` · `SATSANG: WE GO TO KRISHNA TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: A man is walking south, following a light. On pilgrimage in the north, the story says, he sees a glow in the southern sky. He follows it a long way, to a temple town in the Tamil country, to a tamarind tree, and to a young man sitting in a hollow at its foot. Eyes closed. Not speaking. People there say he's been that way since he was a baby. The traveler has one question for him, and it's a riddle.
screen: `A LIGHT IN THE SOUTHERN SKY.` → `A TAMARIND TREE.` → `A YOUNG MAN WHO NEVER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: The young man is Nammalvar, the second name in our title. The traveler is Madhurakavi. Tradition says Nammalvar was born and didn't cry, didn't nurse, didn't open his eyes, and his worried parents left him at the temple, where he sat under the tamarind, growing up in stillness. Madhurakavi asks him, roughly: if a small thing is born inside something dead, what will it eat, and where will it lie? And for the first time, the story says, Nammalvar answers. It will eat that, and it will lie there. Two short lines, and Madhurakavi falls at his feet, his disciple for life. What did they mean? One traditional reading: the small thing is the living self, the atman, born into a body that by itself is lifeless matter. Until it turns to God, it feeds on that body's pleasures and pains, and stays there. That's one of Hinduism's oldest teachings in two lines: you are not your body. The body is where the self lives for now, and the self in it is alive in a way the body isn't. Other teachers take the riddle further, or differently; the tradition lets it stay a little open. Then the silent one starts to sing. His songs, gathered as the Tiruvaymoli, are full of longing for Vishnu. In some, he speaks as a girl pining for her absent lover. Sri Vaishnava tradition holds these songs so high it calls them the Tamil Veda. And Madhurakavi is remembered among the Alvars too, for a short poem in praise of no one but his teacher.
screen: `A CHILD WHO NEVER CRIED.` · `THE RIDDLE: WHAT WILL IT EAT?` · `IT WILL EAT THAT, AND LIE THERE.` · `THE ATMAN: ALIVE INSIDE THE BODY.` · `THE SILENT ONE BEGINS TO SING.`

segments.voice: Rest your eyes low, like the young man under the tree, and sit still enough that your body gets quiet. Feel the breath moving in it. Then notice the one who is noticing the breath. Many Hindu teachers say that watcher is nearer the self than the body is. If you pray, rest in God's presence in that quiet; if you don't, simply stay with the watching for a few breaths.
The Alvars. The Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. Nammalvar is the silent one under the tamarind, who answered a riddle and then sang the Tiruvaymoli.

910.hook: a hunter who worships Shiva all wrong, and all right
910.carry: shiva looks at the love, not the rules
910.howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus in Tamil Nadu honor the Nayanars in temples, often with images of them in a row, and Kannappa is especially remembered at the Shiva temple of Srikalahasti.

segments.voice: Every morning a priest climbs a hill to a small shrine of Shiva, and every morning he finds a mess. Bits of meat on the stone. Flowers that look like they've been in someone's hair. Water spat everywhere. He cleans it, does the worship properly, and goes home upset. Someone is worshiping here, and doing it all wrong.
screen: `A MESS AT SHIVA'S SHRINE.` → `EVERY MORNING, THE SAME.` → `WHO IS DOING THIS?`

segments.voice: Today the path crosses to the Nayanars, the Tamil saints of Shiva. Tradition counts sixty-three, and their lives are told in a long Tamil work, the Periya Puranam. They're kings, housewives, a potter, a washerman, and today, a hunter, Tinnan. Tracking in the hills, he finds the shrine, and something in him breaks open. He knows no rules, so he worships the way a hunter loves. He carries water in his mouth, because he has no pot. He brings flowers in his hair, because his hands hold his bow. And he brings meat he has roasted and tasted first, so only the best goes to Shiva. That's the mess. In the story, Shiva tells the priest in a dream to hide and watch. So the priest is hiding the day the image's eye starts to bleed. Tinnan's herbs don't help, so he takes an arrow, digs out his own eye, and presses it into place. The bleeding stops. Then the image's other eye starts to bleed. Tinnan sets his foot on the spot, to find it once he's blind, and lifts the arrow to his other eye. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and stops him. He's called Kannappa, a name tied to his eye. It isn't a call to harm yourself; if you ever have thoughts like that, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Andal wore the garland first; now a hunter tastes the meat first. In the Gita, Krishna says: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, and I accept it. That's bhakti at its boldest: God looks at the love before the rules. The story didn't change temple rules, but it tells every nervous beginner what matters most, and the priest who knows every rule is the one sent to watch.
screen: `THE NAYANARS: SAINTS OF SHIVA.` · `WATER IN HIS MOUTH, MEAT TASTED FIRST.` · `HIS OWN EYE FOR THE BLEEDING ONE.` · `SHIVA'S HAND STOPS HIM.` · then, large: `GOD LOOKS AT THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Hindus offer what they have: a flower, a leaf, a little water. Today, offer one small thing, even a glass of water, to Shiva, or to God by whatever name you use, the way Kannappa did: no rulebook, full heart. If you don't pray, give one person something small today with your whole attention.
